prize_parts.citation: For discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and its active form, which made possible incretin-based treatment of type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: B003 remains the strongest case on the list, and after the full first-round exchange I rest it on the science, not on the fact that all six of us ranked it first. Holst established GLP-1 secretion and action in humans, Drucker the proglucagon-derived peptide and receptor biology and the therapeutic concept, and Mojsov the identification and synthesis of the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide. Together these are a discovery arc that explains why long-acting agonists work, and it is confirmed by independent outcome trials in diabetes, obesity, and cardiovascular and renal disease. Nobody has raised a maturity concern. A single part with a three-person discovery core is coherent and does not split the achievement. The central appetite-regulating actions of these peptides also make it general physiology, not only a drug story.
statement.case_against: Attribution is still the weak point and the exchange has not removed it. Mojsov's priority for the active peptide against the Habener group, who are not among the credited names, cannot be settled from the supplied record, and I cannot verify it. Leaving out Knudsen means the prize honours the discovery layer and not the medicinal chemistry that produced liraglutide and semaglutide, and that choice needs an explicit rationale. Long-term safety of chronic use is still accruing. A single-part prize also leaves out B015, which I regard as the strongest second candidate but which is not ready, because Eshhar's original chimeric receptor concept is not credited.

responses.point: Perlmann keeps Mojsov but says he would reconsider her seat before replacing discovery with development, and he would accept Knudsen as the third name if Mojsov's contribution cannot be defended. He also ranks B043 second as the cleanest basic-science credit.
responses.response: I have changed my preferred third name since my opening ballot, which preferred Knudsen, and I now agree with his framing: the seat is decided by whether the active-peptide work was decisive, and the record does not show it was not. Dropping Mojsov because her priority is contested, when no one has documented that her contribution was overstated, would substitute convenience for judgment. I accept that the citation must not claim she alone identified the peptide. On B043 I still hold that Walter and Mori are the cleanest attribution on the list, but the PERK and ATF6 arms and the still developing human disease link keep it as an alternative and not a second part this year. I disclose my co-authorship with him.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius says that if the committee prefers a physiology-plus-translation story, Drucker, Holst and Knudsen is defensible, but then Mojsov's omission needs an explicit rationale that her contribution was not decisive, to be settled on the documented record and not on prominence.
responses.response: I accept that test and I think B003 passes it with Mojsov. Her synthesis and characterisation of the active peptide is the step that made the physiology interpretable, and no member has shown that it was not decisive. Her point also tells me that choosing Knudsen would require stating the opposite, and I cannot support that statement on the supplied evidence. I agree with her that B015 is not ready to share this prize because Eshhar's concept is uncredited and solid-tumour efficacy and secondary T-cell malignancy risk remain open, and I therefore do not propose B010 or B015 as a second part. B010 stays below B015 for me because upstream BCR-ABL work and earlier prizes on targeted CML therapy weigh against it.

responses.point: El-Manira argues that Mojsov's identification of the biologically active form made any such drug rational, that a contested priority claim argues for careful citation wording and not for removal, and that Knudsen's medicinal chemistry is development built on the discovery. He also ranks optogenetics (B036) second.
responses.response: I agree with him and have moved to his position on the third seat, as I said in round 1. His point about wording is the one I would act on: the citation says the discoveries concern the physiology of GLP-1 and its active form, and it does not name a single discoverer of the peptide, so it leaves the Habener question to the historical record without misattributing it. I still do not support B036 as a second part, even though I take his view that optogenetics is a transformative causal tool. Six credited names cannot be cut to three without omitting someone with a decisive claim, and a research tool lacks a settled disease-level advance, which is the standard I apply to a second part.

responses.point: Linnarsson regards Knudsen as the best alternative trio but prefers Mojsov because the active-peptide identification is a discovery-stage finding, and he asks that the committee say openly if the credit question cannot be settled instead of replacing her by default. He also notes that six-way convergence may reflect shared reasoning from the same evidence.
responses.response: I agree, and I accept his caution about convergence. Our agreement came from the same supplied evidence, so it is not independent confirmation. That is why I would want the committee's record to state the open priority question plainly, and why I would check the early primary papers on the active peptide before the final vote and not rely on our summaries. I would not drop Mojsov by default. On his B040 case I find the Krainer and Bennett pair clean and the principle general for RNA drugs, but follow-up since approval in 2016 is still short and competing gene therapies exist, so I keep it behind B015 and B043 as an alternative and not a second part.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov's contribution to the active GLP-1 peptide is decisive relative to the Habener group, who are not among the credited names. This cannot be resolved from the supplied material, and I would want primary documentary evidence.
Whether the committee is willing to state an explicit rationale for honouring discovery and not drug development, and so for leaving out Knudsen.
If CAR-T were preferred later, how to credit Eshhar's original chimeric receptor concept, and whether June and Sadelain without Rosenberg is the fairest pair.
statement.conflict_note: Per my profile I have about twenty co-authored works with Thomas Perlmann (dopamine neurons, Nurr1, autophagy) and worked with Paul Greengard as a postdoctoral fellow. None of the credited candidates on the shortlist is linked to me through those connections, so no recusal issue is apparent for B003, B015 or B043. I disclose the Perlmann collaboration because he argues for B043. No new conflict has arisen from the first-round exchange.
